rv.q: Andrew Jackson embraces you with its wit and verve, making a bid for the smartest, sharpest new musical in years.
This irreverent biomusical about America's seventh president is a sugar rush of anachronistic attitude and infectious energy that should connect with younger theatergoers seeking something fresh.
Bloody Bloody never fails to entertain: It stays faithful to the peoples president by making him a crowd-pleaser.
But it is 90 thoroughly audacious, politically savvy, politically incorrect minutes that toggle between a 19th century American history lesson and up-to-the-minute 21st century sensibilities.
The show's irreverent energy and rock-musical format make for an entertaining evening, even if the historical liberties taken are considerable.
With their bloody-good 'Andrew Jackson,' director-librettist Alex Timbers and composer-lyricist Michael Friedman have woven a scathing and topical satire on matters patriotic and political
But this is still one of those shows that capture a moment, an old moment, a new moment.

In tracing a restless young nation's teenage crush on a down-home, rifle-toting maverick (played with omnisexual swagger by Benjamin Walker), this musical suggests that when it comes to selecting their leaders, Americans never outgrew adolescence.
This raucous rock musical about our seventh president is a crude but effective piece of political theater that turns American history into a mosh pit.
So why in the name of the bottom line is this awful play—for it is truly, excruciatingly awful—back for a second go-round?
This production suggests that it might be best not to think too hard about such things; better to have a blast and revel in the glory of the coolest guy at the party.
It sometimes falters, yet never loses it's swagger
Though the magnetic Benjamin Walker is an exhilarating force in the title role, some ensemble members come across as a bit green on an imposing Broadway stage.
It was an intense fifteen minutes that hinted at how powerful the show could be.
Snarky rock musical about 'Old Hickory' is more sophomoric than satiric.
Shows this weird and wonderful don't make it to Broadway every day.
For all his rock-star strutting, he shows us the commoner who became a statesman while grappling with personal and national crises.
But these are my only quibbles with an otherwise riotously funny evening.
The show — a chaotic combination of youthful exuberance, historical fact, populist ideology and gross humor — is likely to confuse and frustrate just as many theatergoers as it appeals to.
But for something lightweight, fresh and fun, "Andrew Jackson" is worth the Benjamins.
We're stuck at an evening hosted by an obnoxious, self-justifying adolescent, never knowing why we should bother about him.
Much as I wished to, I couldn't join them.

But this political burlesque, though energetically acted and featuring a grabby rock score by Michael Friedman, is so overwrought and simpleminded that it quickly becomes a trial to sit through, and something of an insult.
Benjamin Walker is beyond charismatic as Jackson, portraying him more like a rock idol than a crusty Presidential icon.

I disliked the show very much, principally for its deliberate, rampant, and random distortions of the historical record, which strike me as both dangerous and antithetical to the principles America is founded upon.
